title: An isoelectronic series that crosses a period
subtopic: The periodic table: Classification of elements
stem: Five monatomic ions A–E each contain 10 electrons. Their proton numbers are 8, 9, 11, 12 and 13 respectively. The figure gives their radii (140, 133, 102, 72 and 54 pm).

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify A–E, including charges, and explain the radius trend without invoking a change in occupied principal shell.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: A student claims neutral sodium must also be smaller than neutral fluorine. Evaluate the claim using electron configurations.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Deduce the formula of the neutral compound formed by E and A, and predict whether it conducts as a pure solid and when molten.

steps.text: A = O²⁻ and B = F⁻.
C = Na⁺, D = Mg²⁺ and E = Al³⁺.
Each has the same occupied shells and 10 electrons, while nuclear charge increases.
Greater attraction between the nucleus and the same electron population contracts the ion.
Neutral Na is 1s²2s²2p⁶3s¹; neutral F is 1s²2s²2p⁵.
Na has an additional occupied shell with greater distance and shielding, so the ionic-series argument cannot be transferred; neutral Na is larger.
Al₂O₃ follows from balancing 2 × (+3) with 3 × (−2).
The ionic solid has ions fixed in place; molten material has mobile ions and conducts.

title: Ordering halogens from a reaction network
subtopic: The periodic table: Classification of elements
stem: X, Y and Z are chlorine, bromine and iodine in an unknown order. X₂ displaces Y₂ from Y⁻, Y₂ displaces Z₂ from Z⁻, and Z₂ does not react with X⁻. For a separate experiment, 0.0100 mol X₂ is added to excess aqueous Y⁻; the resulting halogen is completely transferred to fresh excess Z⁻.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify X, Y and Z and explain the trend in oxidizing ability in terms of attraction for an incoming electron.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write ionic equations for both stages and determine the final amount of Z₂.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Deduce the overall equation and explain whether Y⁻ is consumed overall.

steps.text: X = chlorine, Y = bromine, Z = iodine.
Oxidizing ability decreases down Group 17 as the incoming electron is added farther from the nucleus and experiences greater shielding.
Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂.
Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂.
0.0100 mol I₂ forms because each stage has a 1:1 halogen mole ratio.
Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂.
Br⁻ is consumed in the first step and regenerated in the second; it is a regenerated halide carrier in the two-stage process, not a net reactant.

title: Solving a mixed oxide composition
subtopic: The periodic table: Classification of elements
stem: A dry 5.0834 g mixture contains only Na₂O and MgO. It is added to excess hydrochloric acid. A back titration shows that 0.2200 mol HCl was consumed. Use M(Na₂O)=61.98 and M(MgO)=40.30 g mol⁻¹. The apparatus sketch shows the mixture being transferred to the acid before the remaining acid is titrated.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write both reactions with HCl and formulate two independent equations for the unknown mole amounts x and y.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the mass percentage of Na₂O.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why measuring only the amount of acid consumed would not determine the composition, and predict the qualitative acid–base character of both oxides.

steps.text: Na₂O + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O; MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O.
Na₂O mass percentage = 36.58% (36.6% accepted).
Each mole of either oxide consumes 2 mol HCl, so acid consumption determines only x + y.
Both are basic metal oxides; oxide ions accept protons to form water.

title: Testing an oxide classification rule
subtopic: The periodic table: Classification of elements
stem: A is ionic Na₂O, B is molecular SO₂, and C is a giant covalent SiO₂ network. C is shown as a fragment of the extended network, with continuation beyond the drawing; the projection does not represent bond angles. A student proposes that an acidic oxide must react with water. Data: A reacts with water to give an alkaline solution; B dissolves to give an acidic solution; C does not react with water but reacts with hot concentrated NaOH to form Na₂SiO₃ and water.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Evaluate the student’s rule and write a balanced equation for C with NaOH.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why water behavior alone cannot establish whether the solid contains discrete molecules.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Compare bonding and charge carriers in molten A and liquid B, and relate the broad metal/nonmetal trend to the oxide classification.

steps.text: C is a counterexample: acid–base classification can be shown by reaction with a base even if the oxide does not react with water.
SiO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂SiO₃ + H₂O.
SO₂ consists of discrete molecules, but SiO₂ has a continuous covalent network.
Water reactivity depends on bond-breaking and reaction feasibility; the absence of dissolution is not proof of neutral oxide character.
Molten A contains mobile Na⁺ and O²⁻ ions and conducts.
Pure liquid SO₂ has no substantial population of mobile ions and is a poor conductor.
Electropositive metals tend to form basic ionic oxides; nonmetal oxides are commonly acidic and covalent. This is a broad trend, not a water-solubility definition.

title: An oxide–peroxide mixture and oxidation states
subtopic: The periodic table: Classification of elements
stem: A 2.0194 g dry mixture of Na₂O and Na₂O₂ reacts completely with excess water. All peroxide is ultimately converted to NaOH and O₂; a drying stage removes water vapor before the gas syringe. The dry O₂ volume is 0.1135 dm³ at STP, where molar gas volume is 22.70 dm³ mol⁻¹. Use M(Na₂O)=61.98 and M(Na₂O₂)=77.98 g mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Write the net peroxide reaction and use the gas volume to determine the peroxide mass percentage.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the total amount of NaOH formed from both components.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain, using oxygen oxidation states, why the peroxide reaction is a disproportionation.

steps.text: 2Na₂O₂ + 2H₂O → 4NaOH + O₂.
m(Na₂O₂) = 0.7798 g, giving 38.62% by mass.
Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH; both components give 2 mol NaOH per mole.
O is −1 in peroxide, −2 in hydroxide and 0 in oxygen gas.
Oxygen from the same initial oxidation state undergoes both reduction and oxidation.

title: A missing alcohol isomer
subtopic: Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds
stem: Three compounds A–C are shown. All are alcohols with molecular formula C₄H₁₀O. The complete set of alcohol constitutional isomers with this formula contains four members. Measured boiling temperatures for the four isomers are 117.7, 108.0, 99.5 and 82.2 °C; the lowest belongs to the most compact, highly branched isomer.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Give IUPAC names and classify the alcohol groups in A–C as primary, secondary or tertiary.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Draw and name the missing isomer and explain why an ether is not a valid answer to this specific request.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student attributes its lowest boiling temperature to an inability to hydrogen-bond. Evaluate this explanation.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A 0.0200 mol mixture contains exactly two distinct alcohols from the complete four-member set and consumes 0.0250 mol of oxygen-transfer equivalents in a quantitative test. The supplied rule is 2 equivalents per primary alcohol, 1 per secondary alcohol and 0 per tertiary alcohol. Determine the possible pairs of classes and their amounts. Does this determine the identity of a primary component?

steps.text: A is butan-1-ol, primary.
B is butan-2-ol, secondary.
C is 2-methylpropan-1-ol, primary.
The missing isomer is (CH₃)₃COH, 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
It is a tertiary alcohol; an ether lacks the hydroxy group required by the specified alcohol class.
It has an O–H bond and lone pairs on oxygen, so it can form intermolecular hydrogen bonds.

All four have the same molecular formula; increased branching reduces effective contact between molecules and weakens dispersion contributions. A lower boiling temperature does not establish the absence of hydrogen bonding.
For primary + secondary, p+s=0.0200 and 2p+s=0.0250, giving p=0.00500 mol and s=0.0150 mol.
For primary + tertiary, 2p=0.0250, giving p=0.0125 mol and t=0.00750 mol.
Secondary + tertiary would consume at most 0.0200 mol equivalents; two primary isomers would consume 0.0400 mol. Both are excluded.
The primary component could be A or C; this test measures class-dependent reaction and does not distinguish the two primary connectivities.

title: When combustion does not identify a homologous series
subtopic: Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds
stem: A and B have the structures shown. Complete combustion of 0.0100 mol of either gives 0.0600 mol CO₂ and 0.0600 mol H₂O. Under the stated test conditions, A reacts rapidly with bromine by addition, whereas B does not. Do not assume that a shared empirical formula establishes a shared functional group.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce the molecular formula from the combustion amounts and reconcile it with both structures.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Give A’s IUPAC name and draw the bromine addition product, retaining the six-carbon chain.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why A and B are structural isomers but are not successive members of one homologous series.

steps.text: Each molecule contains 6 carbon atoms and 12 hydrogen atoms, giving C₆H₁₂.
A contains one C=C bond while B contains a ring; each reduces the hydrogen count by two relative to an acyclic alkane.
A is hex-1-ene.
The product is BrCH₂–CHBr–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃; the C=C becomes C–C and one Br attaches to each former double-bond carbon.
They share the molecular formula but have different atom connectivity.
Successive homologues have the same functional group and differ by CH₂; A and B neither differ by CH₂ nor share the alkene functional group.

title: Same molecular formula, different acid behavior
subtopic: Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds
stem: A and B are shown. Both have formula C₃H₆O₂. Only A reacts with excess NaHCO₃ to give one mole of CO₂ per mole of organic compound. A 0.7400 g sample containing only A and B produces 0.1362 dm³ CO₂ at STP (22.70 dm³ mol⁻¹). Use M(C₃H₆O₂)=74.00 g mol⁻¹. The hydrolysis of B is supplied: HCOOCH₂CH₃ + H₂O ⇌ HCOOH + CH₃CH₂OH.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the functional group in each compound, name A and explain why their empirical formulas are identical.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the mole fraction of A and explain whether the mass fraction differs.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student calls the supplied hydrolysis products isomers of A. Evaluate this claim and identify their functional groups.

steps.text: A contains a carboxyl group and is propanoic acid; B contains an ester group.
Both molecular formulas reduce to empirical formula C₃H₆O₂ because 3, 6 and 2 have no common integer factor greater than 1.
Total amount = 0.7400/74.00 = 0.01000 mol; mole fraction A = 0.6000.
Both have the same molar mass, so the mass fraction is also 0.6000.
HCOOH is a carboxylic acid and CH₃CH₂OH is an alcohol.
Neither has molecular formula C₃H₆O₂, so neither is an isomer of A; hydrolysis changes connectivity by reaction with water rather than rearranging one molecule without changing its formula.

stem: The skeletal structure shown contains one bromo substituent and one C=C bond. A student names it 3-bromohex-4-ene. No stereochemical descriptor is required.

steps.text: 4-bromohex-2-ene.
The six-carbon chain is numbered to give the double bond locant 2 rather than 4; the bromo substituent is then at carbon 4.
The two alkene carbons each carry one H, and the brominated carbon carries one H.
Molecular formula C₆H₁₁Br; it is already the simplest whole-number ratio, so the empirical formula is the same.
For example BrCH₂–CH=CH–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃, i.e. 1-bromohex-2-ene.
An isomer changes connectivity, such as moving the C–Br bond; rotating or reversing a drawing preserves connectivity.

title: Hydrogen-bond evidence and an unfair boiling-point comparison
subtopic: Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds
stem: A, B and C are ethanol, methoxymethane and ethane-1,2-diol respectively, with the structures shown. Their normal boiling temperatures are approximately 78, −24 and 197 °C. A and B have the same molar mass; C does not. Hydrogen bonding requires an H bonded to O, N or F and a lone pair on an appropriate electronegative atom.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why A and B have very different boiling temperatures despite equal molar mass.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Draw one valid hydrogen bond between water and B, labeling the donor and acceptor atoms. Explain why B need not be insoluble in water.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the claim that C’s higher boiling point proves that a hydrogen bond involving C is individually stronger than one involving A.

steps.text: A has an O–H hydrogen-bond donor and oxygen lone-pair acceptor; its molecules hydrogen-bond to one another.
B has acceptor lone pairs but no O–H/N–H/F–H donor, so pure B lacks this hydrogen-bond network.
More energy is required to separate A molecules; dispersion forces alone do not explain the difference.
A valid drawing is O(water)–H···O(B), with the dotted interaction from water H to B oxygen.
Water supplies donors and B supplies acceptors; absence of self hydrogen bonding does not imply absence of hydrogen bonding to water.
C has two hydroxy groups per molecule and can form a more extensive intermolecular network.
C also has higher molar mass and more electrons, affecting dispersion. Bulk boiling data alone do not isolate the strength of an individual hydrogen bond.

subject: chemistry

title: Amine classification is not a count of N–H bonds
subtopic: Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds
stem: Three amines A–C have formula C₃H₉N. Their structures and measured boiling temperatures are A: 49 °C, B: 36 °C, C: 3 °C. Each reacts with HCl by accepting one proton at the nitrogen lone pair. Assume complete protonation with excess HCl.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Classify each amine and distinguish this classification from the number of H atoms bonded to nitrogen.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why C’s low boiling temperature does not prevent it from hydrogen-bonding to water or reacting with HCl.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Determine the HCl amount required to protonate 0.2955 g of any one pure isomer, using molar mass 59.10 g mol⁻¹. Evaluate a student’s proposed 2:1 HCl:A ratio.

steps.text: A is primary: one carbon group on N, with two N–H bonds.
B is secondary: two carbon groups on N, with one N–H bond.
C is tertiary: three carbon groups on N, with no N–H bond.
C has no donor N–H bond for self hydrogen bonding, but its nitrogen lone pair accepts a hydrogen bond from water.
The same lone pair can accept H⁺, giving (CH₃)₃NH⁺.
n(amine)=0.2955/59.10=0.005000 mol, requiring 0.005000 mol HCl.
Each nitrogen has one proton-accepting lone pair; two pre-existing N–H bonds in A do not create two independent basic sites.

subtopic: Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds
stem: A mixture contains only the two C₅H₁₂O alcohols shown. Its total amount is 0.01000 mol. Under the stated quantitative test, each mole of primary alcohol produces one mole of a measured carboxylic acid, while tertiary alcohol is recovered unchanged; 0.006000 mol acid is obtained. Use M(C₅H₁₂O)=88.15 g mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Name and classify A and B, identifying the carbon atom that controls the classification.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the masses of A and B in the initial mixture.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why a combustion carbon/hydrogen ratio would not determine this composition, and why assigning the difference in reactivity simply to stronger intermolecular hydrogen bonding is insufficient.

steps.text: A is pentan-1-ol; its OH-bearing carbon is attached to one carbon, so it is primary.
B is 2-methylbutan-2-ol; its OH-bearing carbon is attached to three carbons, so it is tertiary.
The isomers have identical molecular and empirical formulas, so any mixture has the same combustion carbon/hydrogen ratio.
Both contain O–H groups and can hydrogen-bond; the selective covalent reaction depends on the local bonding at the OH-bearing carbon, including the absence of a carbon-bound H there in B.

title: Two reversals within a periodic ionization trend
subtopic: The periodic table: Classification of elements
stem: First ionization energies across Period 3 are shown: Na 496, Mg 738, Al 578, Si 787, P 1012, S 1000, Cl 1251 and Ar 1521 kJ mol⁻¹. Interpret both downward steps using electron sublevels and electron–electron repulsion.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain the overall increase and the Mg→Al reversal with the relevant valence configurations.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use orbital occupancy to explain the P→S reversal. Do not rely only on a phrase such as “half-filled stability”.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether the graph alone predicts which period-3 element has the greatest second ionization energy. Identify that element using configurations.

steps.text: Across the period nuclear charge increases with broadly similar principal-shell shielding, increasing attraction for valence electrons.
Mg is [Ne]3s² and Al is [Ne]3s²3p¹.
The removed Al electron is in a higher-energy, less penetrating 3p sublevel and is easier to remove than a Mg 3s electron.
P is [Ne]3s²3p³ with one electron in each 3p orbital; S is [Ne]3s²3p⁴ with one 3p pair.
Repulsion between paired electrons in S makes one of those electrons easier to remove, slightly outweighing the increase in nuclear charge.
First and second ionization remove electrons from different species, so the first-ionization graph alone is insufficient.
Na has the greatest second ionization energy: Na⁺ is [Ne], so removal is from the n=2 core rather than the n=3 valence shell of the other period-3 cations.

title: Transition-metal electron states in a catalytic cycle
subtopic: The periodic table: Classification of elements
stem: The two supplied steps are 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂ and 2Fe²⁺ + S₂O₈²⁻ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻. Iron has Z=26. A lower measured activation barrier is observed with the iron catalyst; temperature and reactant concentrations are unchanged.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Give the ground-state electron configurations of Fe, Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺, explaining the order of electron removal.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Add the steps to obtain the overall ionic equation and identify where iron is oxidized and reduced.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain why variable oxidation states enable the cycle and evaluate a claim that the catalyst changes the reaction’s equilibrium constant.

steps.text: Fe is [Ar]3d⁶4s².
Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶ and Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵; the 4s electrons are removed before 3d when these cations form.
S₂O₈²⁻ + 2I⁻ → 2SO₄²⁻ + I₂.
Fe³⁺ is reduced to Fe²⁺ in the iodide step; Fe²⁺ is oxidized in the peroxodisulfate step.
Accessible Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ states permit electron transfer in two steps and regeneration of the catalyst.
The catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, increasing rate.
It does not change the reactant/product energy difference or the equilibrium constant at the same temperature.

title: Ligand color changes without changing oxidation state
subtopic: The periodic table: Classification of elements
stem: Complexes A and B both contain Cu²⁺ but different ligands. Their broad absorption-band maxima are 650 nm (A) and 450 nm (B). The figure illustrates the two probe wavelengths for A; use the stated maxima for the energy calculation. Simplified complementary-color pairs are red↔cyan, orange↔blue, yellow↔violet. Treat 650 nm as red and 450 nm as blue. Use h=6.63×10⁻³⁴ J s, c=3.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹ and Nₐ=6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the Cu²⁺ d-electron count and explain why replacing ligands can change color while Cu remains +2.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the molar photon energies at both maxima and identify the larger splitting.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict the simplified transmitted colors and state one reason a real solution need not match a single complementary color exactly.

steps.text: Cu²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁹, so it is d⁹.
Ligands split the d-orbital energies; different ligands change the splitting and thus the visible photon energy absorbed. A color change need not imply oxidation-state change.
Use E = hcNₐ/λ, with wavelengths converted from nm to m.
A: 184 kJ mol⁻¹; B: 266 kJ mol⁻¹ (three significant figures).
B has the larger splitting because it absorbs shorter-wavelength, higher-energy photons.
A absorbs red, so its simplified transmitted color is cyan; B absorbs blue, so it is orange.
Real absorption bands are broad and may overlap, and perceived color depends on the whole transmitted spectrum and illumination.

stem: MnO₄⁻ is intensely purple and absorbs strongly in the green/yellow region. Its simplified spectrum is shown (relative absorbance at 450, 520, 580, 650 nm: 0.10, 0.90, 0.70, 0.10). steps.text: Removing 4s² and 3d⁵ gives d⁰.
A d⁰ ion has no d electron to undergo a transition between split d levels, so a d–d-only explanation cannot account for this color.
Charge transfer involves an initially occupied ligand-based orbital and can absorb visible light even when the metal d count is zero.
Transition-element classification depends on forming at least one ion with a partially filled d sublevel; Mn²⁺, for example, is d⁵.
The blue/violet and red regions are transmitted more than green/yellow, consistent with purple appearance.

stem: A cobalt compound has composition Co(NH₃)₅Cl₃·xH₂O. The water is crystallization water. A 0.26845 g portion loses 0.01802 g on gentle drying without losing NH₃ or Cl. A fresh equal portion gives 0.28664 g AgCl immediately with excess AgNO₃, when only uncoordinated chloride reacts. After complete breakdown of all complexes, the total AgCl is 0.42996 g. M(AgCl)=143.32, M(H₂O)=18.02, and M(Co(NH₃)₅Cl₃)=250.43 g mol⁻¹. All NH₃ is coordinated.

parts.label: c

steps.text: Dry compound mass = 0.25043 g; amount = 0.25043/250.43 = 0.001000 mol.

Total chloride = 0.003000 mol, so the third chloride is coordinated and unavailable to precipitate immediately.
Formula [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O; the complex cation is [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]²⁺.
Co is +3 because neutral NH₃ plus one Cl⁻ gives complex charge +2; Co³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶.
Coordination number 6: five nitrogen donor atoms and one chloride donor.

subtopic: Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds
stem: An unknown has formula C₄H₈O₂ and a molecular ion at m/z 88. The constructed IR shows a strong 1740 cm⁻¹ absorption and no broad O–H band. Its ¹H NMR has δ1.25 triplet (integral 3), δ4.10 quartet (2), and δ2.00 singlet (3). Candidate structures are CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, CH₃CH₂COOCH₃, HCOOCH(CH₃)₂ and CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH.

steps.text: CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ (ethyl ethanoate).
The ethoxy CH₃ is the δ1.25 triplet (two neighboring H); OCH₂ is the δ4.10 quartet (three neighboring H).
The CH₃ next to C=O gives the δ2.00 singlet, with no adjacent proton-bearing carbon.
The broad acid O–H absorption is absent, inconsistent with the carboxylic-acid candidate.
All four are C₄H₈O₂ isomers and have the same molecular-ion nominal mass 88.
CH₃CO⁺ has nominal mass 2(12)+3+16=43.
The neutral fragment is ·OC₂H₅ with mass 45; atoms, mass 88=43+45, and total charge +1 are conserved.

title: Distinguishing two ethyl groups in an ester
subtopic: Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds
stem: A compound has formula C₅H₁₀O₂ and molecular-ion m/z 102. IR shows an ester C=O near 1740 cm⁻¹ and no broad O–H. The NMR has δ1.00 triplet (3H), δ1.25 triplet (3H), δ2.30 quartet (2H), δ4.15 quartet (2H). Candidate connectivities are CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃, CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃ and CH₃CH₂CH₂COOCH₃.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Deduce the connectivity and assign both CH₂ resonances.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use a specific NMR feature to exclude each alternative, rather than relying only on carbon count.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: An acylium fragment C₃H₅O⁺ appears at m/z 57. Identify the lost neutral radical and verify mass, atom and charge conservation.

steps.text: CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃ (ethyl propanoate).
The δ4.15 quartet is OCH₂, and δ2.30 quartet is CH₂ next to C=O.
Each is adjacent to a CH₃ group, producing quartet splitting; the methyl partners give the two 3H triplets.
CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃ requires an acetyl CH₃ singlet, absent here.
CH₃CH₂CH₂COOCH₃ requires an OCH₃ singlet, absent here.
Lost radical is ·OC₂H₅, nominal mass 45.
C₅H₁₀O₂⁺· → C₃H₅O⁺ + ·OC₂H₅; 102=57+45, all atoms balance and total charge remains +1.

title: A non-racemic mixture that ordinary spectra cannot resolve
subtopic: Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds
stem: A and B are the two drawn enantiomers of butan-2-ol. At the stated temperature, wavelength, total concentration and path length, a pure A solution rotates plane-polarized light by +12.0° and pure B by −12.0°. Mixture rotation is the mole-fraction weighted sum under these same conditions. A mixture gives +3.00°. The measured IR spectra are taken in an achiral environment.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the stereogenic carbon and explain why the drawings represent enantiomers. No R/S labels are required.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the mole percentages of A and B and explain why the mixture is not racemic.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate whether a match in IR spectrum and boiling temperature proves the mixture is racemic.

steps.text: The carbon bonded to OH has four different groups: OH, H, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃.
The drawings have opposite three-dimensional arrangements at this carbon and are non-superimposable mirror images.
Let x be A’s mole fraction: 12.0x − 12.0(1−x)=3.00.
A racemate is 50:50 and has zero net rotation; this sample has excess A.
Enantiomers have the same IR absorption in an achiral environment and the same boiling temperature under the same conditions.
Those observations do not determine their proportions; optical rotation under controlled conditions can distinguish a non-racemic mixture.

title: Why only one alkene connectivity gives cis/trans forms
subtopic: Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds
stem: The three structures A–C are shown. In A the terminal methyl groups lie on opposite sides of C=C; in B they lie on the same side. C has a terminal CH₂= group. Do not use E/Z notation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Name A and B using cis/trans terminology and explain the structural requirement that C fails.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why interconversion of A and B is not ordinary rotation around a single bond, and distinguish their relationship from that between A and C.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student states that equal molecular mass proves all three have identical boiling temperatures. Evaluate the reasoning and identify one feature that can change intermolecular attraction.

steps.text: A is trans-but-2-ene; B is cis-but-2-ene.
Each C of C=C must have two different substituents; the terminal carbon of C (but-1-ene) has two H atoms and fails this requirement.
The π bond constrains rotation; interconversion requires disruption of π overlap rather than free C–C single-bond rotation.
A and B are stereoisomers with the same connectivity; A and C are structural isomers with a different double-bond position.
Equal mass alone does not fix intermolecular forces; spatial arrangement and molecular symmetry can alter resultant dipoles and packing.
The cis and trans arrangements can have different net dipoles, so physical properties may differ even though formula and connectivity match.

title: Counting distinct stereoisomers without double counting
subtopic: Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds
stem: A, B and C are three distinct connectivities with formula C₄H₇Br: A=CH₂=CH–CHBr–CH₃; B=CH₃–CH=CH–CH₂Br; C=CH₂=C(Br)–CH₂–CH₃. Where the drawing leaves stereochemistry unspecified, include all possible stereoisomers. Use cis/trans descriptions where applicable; R/S and E/Z labels are not required.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the stereoisomer count for A, explaining which feature creates it and why its C=C does not create a second pair.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the count for B and C, with a structural reason for each.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: State the total across the three connectivities and explain why an approximately 1:1 molecular-ion pair two mass units apart would not settle which connectivity is present.

steps.text: A has one carbon bonded to Br, H, CH₃ and CH=CH₂, giving two enantiomers.
Its terminal C=C has one carbon with two H atoms, so no cis/trans pair occurs.
B has two cis/trans forms because each alkene carbon carries H and a different carbon group; it has no stereogenic tetrahedral carbon.
C has one form: the terminal C=C fails the two-different-substituents test and no tetrahedral carbon has four different groups.
Total = 2+2+1 = 5 stereoisomers.
Each contains one bromine atom; comparable ⁷⁹Br/⁸¹Br abundances give the same approximate M:M+2 pattern for all three connectivities and their stereoisomers.

title: A nonpolar molecule can absorb infrared radiation
subtopic: Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds
stem: For this problem, a vibration absorbs IR only if the molecular dipole changes during that vibration. CO₂ is linear and has zero permanent dipole. Its symmetric stretch leaves the dipole zero; an asymmetric stretch and bending vibrations change the instantaneous dipole. Bands occur near 2349 and 667 cm⁻¹. Much of Earth’s outgoing thermal radiation lies between 5 and 30 μm. Use λ=1/wavenumber, with consistent units.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why the symmetric stretch can be IR-inactive while the asymmetric stretch and bend are active, despite the same atoms and bonds.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Convert both wavenumbers to wavelengths in μm and identify which falls within the stated 5–30 μm interval.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Evaluate the rule “all nonpolar molecules are IR-inactive” and compare a homonuclear diatomic molecule under the supplied dipole-change criterion.

steps.text: In the symmetric stretch the equal, opposite bond dipoles cancel throughout the vibration, so the dipole does not change.
The other motions break that instantaneous cancellation and change the dipole, permitting absorption under the supplied rule.
λ(667)=10⁴/667=15.0 μm; this is within the stated interval, while 4.26 μm is outside.
CO₂ is a counterexample: a permanent dipole is not required if a vibration changes dipole.
A homonuclear diatomic such as N₂ remains symmetric during its stretch and has no changing dipole, so its stretching vibration is IR-inactive under this model.

title: Quantifying a mixture from whole-multiplet integrals
subtopic: Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds
stem: A mixture contains ethanol and ethanal only, with total amount 0.01000 mol. Its NMR has δ1.20 triplet (integral 9), δ3.70 quartet (6), δ2.20 doublet (6), δ9.80 quartet (2). These are relative whole-multiplet areas, not line heights; exchangeable OH is omitted. IR has broad O–H near 3300 and C=O near 1720 cm⁻¹. Use M(ethanol)=46.07 and M(ethanal)=44.05 g mol⁻¹. Assume no exchange or reaction between the components during measurement.

parts.label: a

parts.label: b

steps.text: Ethanol CH₃ gives δ1.20 triplet; ethanol CH₂ gives δ3.70 quartet.
Ethanal CH₃ gives δ2.20 doublet because it has one neighboring aldehyde H.
Ethanal CHO gives δ9.80 quartet because it has three neighboring methyl H.
Methyl comparison: (9/3):(6/3)=3:2 for ethanol:ethanal.
CH₂/CHO comparison: (6/2):(2/1)=3:2, confirming the ratio.
Amounts are ethanol 0.006000 mol and ethanal 0.004000 mol.
Different functional groups have different absorption strengths and band shapes; no common proportionality calibration from IR depth to component amount was supplied.

title: Reconciling exchange, integration and a molecular formula
subtopic: Functional groups: Classification of organic compounds
stem: An alcohol has molecular formula C₃H₈O and molecular-ion m/z60. Before adding D₂O, its ¹H NMR contains a 6H doublet near δ1.20, a 1H CH resonance near δ3.90 whose splitting is deliberately unresolved in the figure, and a broad exchangeable 1H signal. After D₂O treatment the broad 1H signal disappears but the other integrated areas remain 6:1. Compare propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol. No interpretation of higher-order multiplets is required.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Identify the alcohol and explain the 6H doublet without interpreting the unresolved CH resonance.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the D₂O result supports the functional-group assignment, and reconcile all eight H atoms with the formula.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Propose an atom- and charge-balanced fragmentation giving C₃H₇⁺ at m/z43 from the molecular radical cation. Explain whether this fragment alone distinguishes the two alcohol isomers.

steps.text: Propan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂CHOH.
Two equivalent methyl groups give six H in one environment; one adjacent CH proton splits their signal into a doublet.
The disappearing broad proton is an exchangeable O–H hydrogen, consistent with an alcohol.
There are six methyl H, one methine H and one OH H, giving eight in total.
C₃H₈O⁺· → C₃H₇⁺ + ·OH; nominal masses 60=43+17 and total charge +1 is conserved.
The fragment formula can be formed by loss of OH from either isomer, so this fragment alone does not establish the original connectivity; the NMR evidence does.
